brief: Gold has bounced over two sessions but stays rangebound, trading near late-March levels and below its 200-day moving average, with no medium-term trend. Gold has effectively traded as a dollar proxy this year; the dollar's inverted overshoot reset after the FOMC. Higher rates weigh on rate-sensitive ETF demand, but Goldman argues the latest Fed tightening should slow gold's appreciation path rather than change its longer-term destination, since much of the expected tightening is already reflected in ETF holdings; GS still targets $4,650 by year-end versus about $4,350 currently. Central banks, unlike ETF investors, do not react to rates or the dollar: Goldman's nowcast puts central-bank buying at about 91 tonnes per month (three-month seasonally adjusted) versus a pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes, and GS has raised its assumed 2026-27 buying pace accordingly. Demand for gold calls runs about three times historical averages, so if the dollar rolls over and gold breaks higher, dealer hedging could amplify the move. Tactically stuck, structurally strong: not a chase now, but the eventual breakout could be sharp.
